title: A Self-Consistent Two-Carrier Drift-Diffusion Framework for p-n Junctions: Extended Diode Equation, Power Dissipation, and Base Transit Time
authors: Jianhong Yang, Tinglan Li, Gonghao Sun
abstract: The classical theory of p-n junctions derives the current-voltage characteristic from minority-carrier diffusion alone: majority carriers are treated as an inert background, the quasi-neutral base as field-free, and the junction voltage as equal to the applied bias. These premises fail together under high bias and high-level injection, where the observed current roll-off is reproduced only by appending an empirical series resistance outside the junction physics. Here we develop a self-consistent two-carrier drift-diffusion framework that introduces no assumption beyond the classical ones. Excess majority carriers are shown to be electrostatically forced transport participants: the ambipolar diffusion equation, closed by exact two-sided boundary conditions, yields a unified excess-carrier profile. The resulting base field separates into an ohmic and a Dember component, and all four current components follow in closed form, their sum being position independent. At device level the framework closes into an extended diode equation that contains the Shockley equation as its low-injection, long-base limit and reproduces the n=2 roll-off intrinsically. The junction voltage emerges as a self-limiting drop confined to the space-charge region and separated from the applied bias by exact base drops. Two device-level corrections are quantified: at high current, 75-90% of the dissipation migrates from the junction into the quasi-neutral base, and field-assisted acceleration shortens the base transit time by up to a factor of six. Three parameter-free predictions follow: a universal ideality-factor crossover that passes through 3/2 when the boundary excess equals the doping, a high-injection onset voltage that scales as 119 mV per decade of doping, and a geometry factor that survives into high injection.
summary: This paper presents a self-consistent two-carrier drift-diffusion model to correct the classical understanding of p-n junctions under extreme bias. It derives an extended diode equation that accurately predicts current roll-off and quantifies how power dissipation shifts into the base region. The work provides several parameter-free, testable predictions for semiconductor device physics.
main_problem: Classical p-n junction theory fails under high bias and high-level injection because it neglects the role of majority carriers and treats the junction voltage incorrectly.
main_result: The authors develop a self-consistent two-carrier drift-diffusion framework yielding an extended diode equation that intrinsically reproduces high-injection current roll-off and accurately quantifies power dissipation partitioning.
method: The framework solves the coupled ambipolar diffusion equation for excess carrier profiles, leading to closed-form expressions for all current components and the junction voltage.
model_or_system: The study models p-n junctions in semiconductor devices, treating excess majority and minority carriers as coupled transport participants governed by drift-diffusion equations.
key_observables: Extended diode equation, junction voltage drop, power dissipation partitioning (75-90% into base), and base transit time.
important_parameters: High bias/high injection regime, doping concentration ($N$), base width ($W$), and diffusion lengths ($L_a$).
main_assumptions: The framework assumes the quasi-neutrality condition ($\delta_n \approx \delta_p$) and neglects higher-order terms like ambipolar drift, though these are shown to be small corrections.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the hyperbolic profile of excess carriers ($\delta(x)$) unifying long-base and short-base limits, and show the coupling of boundary excess concentrations to the single junction voltage $V_j$.
paper_structure: The paper develops the two-carrier description, derives the extended diode equation, and then dedicates sections to quantifying power dissipation and base transit time corrections.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state devices, the rigorous derivation of transport equations and the identification of fundamental, universal scaling laws (like the ideality-factor crossover) demonstrate powerful techniques for solving coupled, non-linear transport systems.
